items.followUp: Why do molten ionic compounds conduct electricity?

rubric.why: Identifies the mobile charged particles present when an ionic compound dissolves.
rubric.description: The compound separates into positive and negative ions in solution.
rubric.how: State that positive and negative ions are present and able to move in solution.

rubric.why: Explains how ions make the solution conduct electricity.
rubric.description: Moving ions carry electric charge and conduct electricity.
rubric.how: Link the movement of ions to the carrying of electric charge or electrical conduction.

modelAnswer: In aqueous solution, an ionic compound separates into positive and negative ions that can move freely.
These moving ions carry electric charge, so the solution conducts electricity.

items.followUp: What is a double covalent bond? Give an example.

rubric.why: The number of shared electron pairs defines a triple covalent bond.
rubric.description: A triple covalent bond forms when two atoms share three pairs of electrons.
rubric.how: State that three pairs of electrons are shared between the bonded atoms.

rubric.why: A suitable example demonstrates a triple covalent bond.
rubric.description: A nitrogen molecule (N₂) has a triple covalent bond.
rubric.how: Give nitrogen, N₂, as an example.

modelAnswer: A triple covalent bond forms when two atoms share three pairs of electrons.
A nitrogen molecule (N₂) has a triple covalent bond.

items.followUp: What is meant by a complete valence shell?

rubric.why: Identifies the electron shell relevant to atomic stability.
rubric.description: An atom is stable when its outermost (valence) shell is complete.
rubric.how: State that the atom’s outermost or valence shell is complete or full.

rubric.description: This arrangement is usually an octet, or a duplet in the first shell, like that of a noble gas.
rubric.how: Mention an octet, duplet, or noble-gas arrangement.

modelAnswer: An atom is stable when its outermost (valence) electron shell is complete.
This stable arrangement is usually an octet, or a duplet in the first shell, like that of a noble gas.

items.followUp: Define a solute and give an example of a solute dissolved in water.

rubric.why: Water must be identified as the solvent for a solution to be aqueous.
rubric.description: An aqueous solution is a solution in which water is the solvent.
rubric.how: Define an aqueous solution by stating that water is its solvent.

rubric.why: A correct example applies the definition.
rubric.description: Salt dissolved in water is an example of an aqueous solution.
rubric.how: Give salt, sodium chloride, or sugar dissolved in water as an example.

modelAnswer: An aqueous solution is a solution in which water is the solvent.
For example, salt dissolved in water forms an aqueous solution.

items.followUp: Describe one observation from Rutherford's alpha-particle scattering experiment and state what it showed about the atom.

rubric.why: Identifies the experiment used to investigate atomic structure.
rubric.description: Rutherford directed alpha particles at a thin gold foil and detected them on a fluorescent screen.
rubric.how: Describe the alpha-particle beam and the gold foil, or identify the detecting screen.

rubric.why: Records the observation for most of the alpha particles.
rubric.description: Most alpha particles passed straight through the foil without deflection.
rubric.how: State that most particles passed through with no deflection.

rubric.why: Records the observation for some of the alpha particles.
rubric.description: Some alpha particles were deflected from their paths.
rubric.how: State that some particles were deflected or changed direction.

rubric.why: Records the rare backward or large-angle scattering.
rubric.description: A very few alpha particles were deflected backwards or through large angles.
rubric.how: State that very few particles bounced back or were deflected through a large angle.

modelAnswer: Rutherford directed a narrow beam of alpha particles from a radioactive source at a thin gold foil.
A fluorescent zinc sulphide screen around the foil detected the paths of the particles.
Most alpha particles passed straight through the foil without deflection.
Some particles were deflected, while a very few were deflected backwards.

items.followUp: Explain how magnesium and oxygen form an ionic bond in magnesium oxide.

rubric.why: States the defining force in an ionic bond.
rubric.description: An ionic bond is the electrostatic force of attraction between oppositely charged ions.
rubric.how: Define the bond as the attraction between positive and negative ions.

rubric.why: Describes the electron transfer in the sodium chloride example.
rubric.description: A sodium atom transfers its outer electron to a chlorine atom.
rubric.how: State that sodium transfers, loses, or donates an electron.

rubric.why: Identifies the ions formed by electron transfer.
rubric.description: Sodium becomes a positive sodium ion and chlorine becomes a negative chloride ion.
rubric.how: Identify the positive sodium ion and negative chloride ion.

rubric.why: Connects the attraction between ions to the ionic compound formed.
rubric.description: The oppositely charged ions attract each other to form sodium chloride (NaCl).
rubric.how: State that the ions attract and form sodium chloride.

modelAnswer: An ionic bond is the electrostatic force of attraction between oppositely charged ions.
In sodium chloride formation, a sodium atom transfers its outer electron to a chlorine atom.
Sodium becomes a positive sodium ion (Na⁺), and chlorine becomes a negative chloride ion (Cl⁻).
The oppositely charged ions attract each other to form sodium chloride (NaCl).
